title: "The helpers of the workspace"
subtitle: "Fitting specifications with `try_spec()`"
---





The specifications of the exercise in the Housing and racial bias case study are fitted with helper functions, which are introduced here. The page assumes the R taught in [Getting started with R](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html), the module on the umbrella site of the workshop, written on the data of this case study, up to [section 10](https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds/tools/r.html#sec-shares), in which the share of replies that greeted the sender by name is computed for two groups of names and the difference between the two shares is taken.

The code on this page ran when the page was built, and what R printed appears under each block, which allows you to compare your own output with the page line by line. Type each block into the [workspace](../tracks/day/before.qmd#the-workspace) that you downloaded, or, if your installation fails, into the [browser lab](../lab.qmd), where the helpers are already loaded.

## A first look at `try_spec()` {#sec-try-spec}

The workspace holds a file of helper functions, `R/spec_tools.R`, which the exercise loads once and then uses to fit specifications. A **specification** is one complete set of choices for an analysis, fixing which names are compared, which emails are counted, what happens to the uncoded replies, which model is fitted and which covariates it includes. `source()` runs the file and makes its functions available in your session. In the browser lab the helpers are already loaded, and the line is not needed.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
source("R/spec_tools.R")
```
:::




`try_spec()` fits one specification and prints its result. Every argument has a default, the defaults together making up the reference specification, the comparison made by hand in section 10 of Getting started with R, and calling the function with no arguments therefore reproduces the gap computed there:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
try_spec()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

  comparison=white population=replies uncoded=drop model=lpm adjust=none
  Greeted by name: Hispanic names 41.2% of 187 replies, white names 61.1% of 175
  Difference: -19.97 percentage points, 95% interval -30.12 to -9.81
  Test: t = -3.87 on 360 df, p = 0.00013 (linear probability model, HC2 standard errors)
  n = 362 replies, partial r = -0.200 (the conversion rule of the robustness study)
  Verdict: below zero and significant at 5%, in the direction of the claim
  On the curve: 0 of the 64 specifications have an estimate further below zero
```


:::
:::


The first lines repeat the two shares and their difference, −19.97 points, now with a 95% interval around it. The test line comes from a linear probability model, explained in the [binary-outcomes module](binary-outcomes.qmd), which regresses the 0/1 outcome on an indicator of the Hispanic names and whose coefficient is exactly the difference in shares. The last lines give the number of replies analysed, a partial correlation computed by the rule used in the SCORE robustness study (Aczel et al. 2026), the class of the result, and its place among the 64 specifications on the curve of the claim.

Changing one argument changes one decision, and `population = "all"`, for instance, counts every delivered email, as the second calculation of that section does:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
try_spec(population = "all")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```

  comparison=white population=all uncoded=drop model=lpm adjust=none
  Greeted by name: Hispanic names 21.6% of 356 delivered emails, white names 35.0% of 306
  Difference: -13.34 percentage points, 95% interval -20.21 to -6.47
  Test: t = -3.81 on 660 df, p = 0.00015 (linear probability model, HC2 standard errors)
  n = 662 delivered emails, partial r = -0.147 (the conversion rule of the robustness study)
  Verdict: below zero and significant at 5%, in the direction of the claim
  On the curve: 32 of the 64 specifications have an estimate further below zero
```


:::
:::


Options that are not on the curve are refused, with the reason and the page of the workshop site on which they are taught. In the call below the outcome is set to any reply instead of a greeting by name, which would answer a different claim:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
try_spec(outcome = "reply")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error}

```
Error:
! Not on the curve of 64 specifications: outcome = "reply" (Any reply).
  Why: A different claim of the same paper, about whether officials reply at all.
  Taught in: Specification curve, https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/curve.html
  All decisions and options: Decision map, https://codemoreh.github.io/ar4ds-housing/menu.html#map
  On the curve: outcome = "named".
```


:::
:::


Every call to `try_spec()` is logged, and `my_experiments()` prints the log, showing only the decisions that you varied:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
my_experiments()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Specifications tried: 2 (estimates in percentage points)

 population estimate      interval      test       p   n
    replies   -19.97 -30.1 to -9.8 t = -3.87 0.00013 362
        all   -13.34 -20.2 to -6.5 t = -3.81 0.00015 662

Estimates from -19.97 to -13.34 points  |  below zero and significant at 5%: 2 of 2
```


:::
:::


These steps amount to the whole of Task 4 in miniature, in which you change one decision at a time, read what moves and keep a record. The [specification menu](../menu.qmd) lists every argument and its options, while the [cheatsheet](../cheatsheet.qmd) gathers the helpers on one page.
